variants.title: Drive the loop
variants.context: A production execution loop has named transitions: bind the goal contract, propose one step, authorize and execute, validate the observation, then persist or stop with a machine-readable reason. The planner proposes and the deterministic runtime decides.
variants.prompt: A support agent is asked to resolve one case. Put the loop stages in order.

items.text: Propose a step: ask the planner for one structured action or a terminal response.
Validate the observation: treat tool output as untrusted data, check schema and provenance, and reconcile domain state.
Bind the goal: record the target object, allowed scope, success evidence, and prohibited effects before planning.
Authorize and execute: validate the tool, arguments, identity, budget, and approval rule before a credential is used.
Persist or stop: checkpoint progress, then complete, wait, retry within policy, or stop with a machine-readable reason.

variants.hint: Ask which stage is allowed to spend a credential.
variants.explanation: The model proposes one step at a time, and a deterministic runtime decides what executes, what persists, and when to stop.

variants.title: Drive the loop
variants.context: A production execution loop has named transitions: bind the goal contract, propose one step, authorize and execute, validate the observation, then persist or stop with a machine-readable reason. The planner proposes and the deterministic runtime decides.
variants.prompt: A code-fixing agent runs a test tool whose output claims that every check passed. Put the stages in order.

items.text: The runtime checks the tool allowlist, arguments, identity, and budget before the sandbox credential is used.
The planner proposes one structured action: run the test suite on the current branch.
The goal contract already defines success as a green run recorded in the repository, not a claim in a message.
The run checkpoints the verified result and completes, because environment evidence matches the success contract.
The returned output is validated against its schema and compared with the authoritative run record.

variants.hint: A fluent claim of success is not the same as outcome evidence.
variants.explanation: Outcome grading reads authoritative environment state, which is how a false-success claim is caught.

variants.title: Drive the loop
variants.context: A production execution loop has named transitions: bind the goal contract, propose one step, authorize and execute, validate the observation, then persist or stop with a machine-readable reason. The planner proposes and the deterministic runtime decides.
variants.prompt: A run proposes a refund larger than the policy cap for automatic execution. Put the stages in order.

items.text: The run checkpoints the exact pending call, enters waiting_for_approval, and releases the worker without executing.
The goal contract marks financial writes above the cap as effects that require approval.
The planner proposes the refund as one structured action with explicit arguments.
The policy runtime holds the call, because the approval rule for this effect has not been satisfied.

variants.hint: Approval is a stage of the loop, not an interruption of it.
variants.explanation: A durable run persists the pending call before a long wait so no effect executes and no worker is held open.

variants.title: Record the run state
variants.context: Durable state lets a resumed worker prove what was proposed, approved, attempted, and committed. A run moves through created, running, waiting_for_approval, and recovering, and ends in a terminal state such as completed, failed, cancelled, or budget_exhausted.
variants.prompt: A refund run pauses for approval, and its worker dies during the write. Put the recorded states in order.

items.text: completed: authoritative outcome evidence satisfies the success contract.
waiting_for_approval: the exact pending call is durable and no effect has executed.
recovering: a new worker reconciles the interrupted write before deciding anything else.
running: one worker holds the lease and may propose work.
created: the goal contract exists and no execution has started.

variants.hint: Which state exists only because something was interrupted?
variants.explanation: Named states make the difference between success, waiting, recovery, and abandonment visible to an operator.

variants.title: Record the run state
variants.context: Durable state lets a resumed worker prove what was proposed, approved, attempted, and committed. A run moves through created, running, waiting_for_approval, and recovering, and ends in a terminal state such as completed, failed, cancelled, or budget_exhausted.
variants.prompt: A research run keeps proposing lookups until its tool call budget is gone. Put the recorded states in order.

items.text: running: the next proposal is refused because the tool call budget for this run is already spent.
created: the goal contract, budgets, and tool allowlist are recorded before any work begins.
budget_exhausted: a terminal stop reason is written so an operator can see exactly why the run ended.
running: a worker takes the lease, and the runtime counts every proposal and tool call it makes.

variants.explanation: A budget is enforced by the runtime, and exhausting it is a terminal state with its own recorded reason.

variants.title: Record the run state
variants.context: Durable state lets a resumed worker prove what was proposed, approved, attempted, and committed. A run moves through created, running, waiting_for_approval, and recovering, and ends in a terminal state such as completed, failed, cancelled, or budget_exhausted.
variants.prompt: An operator stops a run that is waiting on a reviewer. Put the recorded states in order.

items.text: cancelled: the operator stops the run and the terminal reason is recorded beside the unexecuted call.
created: the run exists with its contract, but nothing has executed.
waiting_for_approval: the pending call is durable, the worker is released, and no effect has run.
running: a worker proposes a sensitive write and the policy runtime requires approval.

variants.hint: Which state exists only because something was interrupted?
variants.explanation: Cancellation is checked between effects, so a stopped run ends with a recorded reason and no half-applied write.

variants.title: Count the budget
variants.context: The runtime counts limits, not the prompt. A declarative policy sets independent budgets such as maxSteps, maxToolCalls, and maxWallClockSeconds, and each one protects a different resource or failure mode.
variants.prompt: A tool authority policy sets maxToolCalls to 6. The run has already made 4 tool calls, and the planner proposes a step that needs 3 more. How many of those proposed calls does the runtime refuse?
variants.hint: Work out how many of the proposed calls still fit under the ceiling.
variants.explanation: 6 minus 4 leaves room for 2 calls, so 1 of the 3 proposed calls exceeds maxToolCalls and is refused.

mistakes.feedback: That is the whole proposed step; two of its calls still fit inside the budget.
That is how many calls are still allowed, not how many are refused.

variants.title: Count the budget
variants.context: The runtime counts limits, not the prompt. A declarative policy sets independent budgets such as maxSteps, maxToolCalls, and maxWallClockSeconds, and each one protects a different resource or failure mode.
variants.prompt: A policy sets maxWallClockSeconds to 90. The run has used 62 seconds, and the next tool call may take up to 20 seconds. How many seconds are left for verification and checkpointing after that call?
variants.hint: Subtract both the time already spent and the worst case for the next call.
variants.explanation: 90 minus 62 minus 20 leaves 8 seconds, which is why a wall-clock budget is checked before each attempt rather than after.

mistakes.feedback: That is the time left before the tool call, not after it.
Subtract the elapsed time from the deadline, not the tool timeout.

variants.title: Count the budget
variants.context: The runtime counts limits, not the prompt. A declarative policy sets independent budgets such as maxSteps, maxToolCalls, and maxWallClockSeconds, and each one protects a different resource or failure mode.
variants.prompt: A policy sets maxSteps to 12, and the runtime counts one step per model turn and one step per tool call. The run has recorded 5 model turns and 4 tool calls. How many steps remain?
variants.hint: Add everything the runtime counts as a step before subtracting.
variants.explanation: 5 turns plus 4 tool calls is 9 of the 12 steps, so 3 remain. Model turns and tool calls are counted by the same limit here.

mistakes.feedback: That counts only the model turns against the budget.
That counts only the tool calls against the budget.

variants.title: Bind the approval
variants.context: An approval gate pauses a durable run before a sensitive call. The reviewer sees canonical server-generated details, and the approval binds to that exact call ID. If the arguments change, the approval is no longer valid.
variants.prompt: A reviewer approves a 40 USD refund. The planner then re-plans and proposes 90 USD on the same case with the same tool. What should the runtime do?
options: Request a new approval, because approval binds to the exact reviewed call.
Execute it, since the approved tool and case are unchanged.
Execute it after confirming 90 USD is still under the policy cap.
optionFeedback: Right: changed arguments invalidate the approval, so this call needs its own decision.
The reviewer authorized an amount, not just a tool name.
A policy cap bounds what may be approved; it does not supply the approval.
variants.hint: Ask exactly what the reviewer agreed to.
variants.explanation: Approval binds to one call ID and its arguments, so any change to those arguments voids it.

variants.title: Bind the approval
variants.context: An approval gate pauses a durable run before a sensitive call. The reviewer sees canonical server-generated details, and the approval binds to that exact call ID. If the arguments change, the approval is no longer valid.
variants.prompt: An approval screen renders the arguments as the model described them in its message rather than from the run record. What is the flaw?
options: The message is longer than the structured call, so reviewers skim it.
The description is not versioned alongside the prompt that produced it.
The reviewer may approve something different from the call that executes.
optionFeedback: Length is a usability issue, not the reason the screen cannot be trusted.
Versioning helps later diagnosis but does not fix what the reviewer sees now.
Right: the reviewer must see canonical server-generated details for the exact call, including target, scope, and reversibility.
variants.hint: Ask exactly what the reviewer agreed to.
variants.explanation: The gate must show server-generated details of the pending call, because model prose is not the artifact that will execute.

variants.title: Bind the approval
variants.context: An approval gate pauses a durable run before a sensitive call. The reviewer sees canonical server-generated details, and the approval binds to that exact call ID. If the arguments change, the approval is no longer valid.
variants.prompt: A planner labels a record deletion as low risk and high confidence, and asks the runtime to skip the approval gate. What should the policy do?
options: Skip approval but log the decision for review afterwards.
Skip approval, since the planner holds the most context about the case.
Require approval, because the policy keys on the actual effect class.
optionFeedback: Logging an unauthorized irreversible effect does not undo it.
The component being constrained cannot be the one that decides the constraint.
Right: approval policy is based on the effect an action has, not on the model's stated confidence.
variants.hint: Ask exactly what the reviewer agreed to.
variants.explanation: Approval policy is derived from the declared effect class, so a model's confidence can never lower the gate.

variants.title: Match the recovery
variants.context: Recovery matches the effect. A read may be retried with backoff, an ambiguous write is reconciled by operation ID, a reversible write is compensated, an irreversible effect is staged and approved, and a partial workflow resumes from a versioned checkpoint.
variants.prompt: A worker dies halfway through a five-step deployment workflow. How should the run continue?
options: Replay every step with a new operation key so each one is fresh.
Restart from the original prompt and hope the planner repeats the path.
Resume from the versioned checkpoint recording the last completed step.
optionFeedback: A new key represents a new effect, so the finished steps would run a second time.
A model rerun is not guaranteed to reproduce the same path, and completed effects would repeat.
Right: a partial workflow resumes from durable state, which is why checkpoints follow every external result.
variants.hint: Name the effect first, then choose the recovery that fits it.
variants.explanation: Partial multi-step work resumes from a versioned checkpoint instead of restarting from the prompt.

variants.title: Match the recovery
variants.context: Recovery matches the effect. A read may be retried with backoff, an ambiguous write is reconciled by operation ID, a reversible write is compensated, an irreversible effect is staged and approved, and a partial workflow resumes from a versioned checkpoint.
variants.prompt: A reversible write committed the wrong value, and the error is found an hour later. What is the right recovery?
options: Run the audited compensation operation for the recorded effect.
Replay the same write, since the operation key makes it idempotent.
Delete the checkpoint so the run can be replayed from a clean state.
optionFeedback: Right: a reversible write is checkpointed precisely so a compensating operation can undo it with an audit trail.
Replaying the same key repeats the wrong value instead of correcting it.
Discarding the evidence removes the only record of what has to be undone.
variants.hint: Name the effect first, then choose the recovery that fits it.
variants.explanation: Reversible writes are compensated through an audited operation, not corrected by replaying the original call.

variants.title: Match the recovery
variants.context: Recovery matches the effect. A read may be retried with backoff, an ambiguous write is reconciled by operation ID, a reversible write is compensated, an irreversible effect is staged and approved, and a partial workflow resumes from a versioned checkpoint.
variants.prompt: A run must send an irreversible legal notice to a customer. What should the design do before it executes?
options: Allow it under a retry policy with backoff and an idempotency key.
Stage or preview the notice, require approval, and reduce the authority.
Allow it, then send a correcting message if the notice turns out wrong.
optionFeedback: Retry policy protects against transient failure and does nothing about permanence.
Right: rollback may be impossible, so the controls have to sit ahead of execution.
A follow-up message does not undo a notice that was already delivered.
variants.hint: Name the effect first, then choose the recovery that fits it.
variants.explanation: Irreversible effects are staged, approved, and run with reduced authority, because no recovery exists afterwards.
